title: Building a Business While Working Full-Time with Nami Prakash
guestBio: Nami Prakash is the founder of The Mind Quotient, a framework and community built around developing human skills for an increasingly automated world. She built her methodology alongside a corporate career and motherhood, bringing her ideas into her teams before ever launching publicly. She is also a memoir writer and single mother whose work sits at the intersection of emotional intelligence, leadership, and personal conviction.
excerpt: Nami Prakash didn't quit her corporate job the moment she had a good idea — she built The Mind Quotient deliberately, tested it inside her teams, and learned the hard way what readiness actually looks like. In this conversation, she and Aimee unpack what it means to carry an idea alongside a full life — and when you'll know it's time to leap.
metaDescription: Nami Prakash shares how she built The Mind Quotient alongside corporate work and motherhood — and what she learned from leaping before she was ready.
keyTakeaways: Building a business while employed full-time is a legitimate and often smarter strategy than quitting before you have proof your idea works.
Readiness to leap is about more than having a name, a mission, and a polished website — it requires tested ideas, real relationships, and honest feedback.
Managing your energy is just as important as managing your time, especially when you are building something new alongside a life that is already full.
Hiding inside endless revisions is not the same as moving deliberately — at some point, you have to put the idea in front of real people.
Inherited expectations about success — from family, culture, or industry — can quietly shape the business you build unless you examine them on your own terms.
MQ Circles are designed to move learning beyond concept and into community: a skill, a guided conversation, and a way to integrate that learning into everyday life.
Setting clear boundaries around work you care deeply about is not a limitation — it is what makes sustainable, meaningful building possible as a single mother and founder.

pullQuotes.text: Moving deliberately is not the same as endlessly revising a website. At some point, the idea has to meet a real person.
I tried to make the leap before I was ready — and that experience taught me more about what readiness actually means than any success could have.
The belief behind everything I build is that human skills are not soft — they are the hardest and most important thing we can develop.
Boundaries are not about protecting yourself from your ambition. They're about protecting the conditions that make your ambition sustainable.

quiz.title: What Kind of Builder Are You?
quiz.description: You have an idea you can't stop thinking about — but ideas don't build themselves, and neither does readiness. This quiz helps you understand your natural building style: the strengths you already have, the edges worth watching, and what your next move might look like. There are no wrong answers. Answer as honestly as you can.

A.name: The Steady Architect
A.description: You build with intention and structure, and you rarely move before you feel ready. Your instinct to be thoughtful protects you from costly mistakes — and it also means the world sometimes doesn't get to see your work as soon as it could. The key insight for you is learning to distinguish deliberate movement from revision as avoidance. Nami's story will resonate deeply with you, because she learned this distinction from the inside out — and came out the other side with a methodology that works.

B.name: The Brave Leaper
B.description: You move fast, trust your gut, and have probably started more things than most people in your circle — some of which landed, some of which didn't. Your boldness is a genuine asset, but this episode will challenge you to ask whether speed is always the same as readiness. Nami's honest account of leaping too early, and what she learned from it, is the kind of story that doesn't diminish brave people — it makes them more strategic.

C.name: The Quiet Carrier
C.description: You have been holding an idea for a while — long enough that it feels almost embarrassingly overdue. You are thoughtful, private about your ambitions, and cautious about who gets to see your unfinished work. Nami's approach to testing ideas in small, low-stakes ways before any public leap was designed for someone exactly like you. This episode gives you permission to move without having everything figured out first.

D.name: The Integrated Builder
D.description: You are building something meaningful, and you are doing it alongside a full life — a job, a family, relationships, responsibilities that don't pause for your ambition. You are not looking for permission to want more; you are looking for a smarter way to carry it all. Nami is speaking directly to you in this episode, and the framework she has built — around energy, feedback, community, and belief — was forged in exactly the conditions you are navigating right now.

questions.question: When you have an idea you're excited about, what do you do first?

options.text: I research, map it out, and build a plan before I tell anyone.
I share it immediately — talking it through helps me figure out if it's real.
I sit with it privately for a long time before I feel ready to surface it.
I look for one small way to test it within the life I already have.

questions.question: How do you tend to think about the timing of a big move?

options.text: I wait until I feel genuinely ready — I'd rather be late than underprepared.
I believe the right time is usually now — conditions are never perfect.
I worry that I'm waiting too long, but I still can't quite make myself move.
I try to make the move sustainable within my current circumstances, not in spite of them.

questions.question: What is your honest relationship with feedback on your work?

options.text: I prefer to refine it privately before I let anyone weigh in.
I love it — the more people I can get it in front of, the better.
I want it, but asking for it makes me feel exposed in ways that are hard to explain.
I seek it strategically — I want feedback from the right people at the right stage.

questions.question: When you think about building something bigger than your current life, what feels most true?

options.text: I want to build it right, even if that takes longer than other people think it should.
I want to build it fast, while I still have the momentum and the nerve.
I want to build it, but I'm not sure I've given myself full permission yet.
I want to build it in a way that doesn't require me to abandon the life I already love.

questions.question: How do you manage your energy when you are working on something that matters to you?

options.text: I protect my planning time fiercely and treat deep work as non-negotiable.
I push hard when the momentum is there and recover afterward.
I struggle with it — I often give my best energy to obligations and leave scraps for my own work.
I am deliberate about which hours and which tasks get my best capacity.

questions.question: What does success look like to you at this stage of building?

options.text: A finished, polished thing I am genuinely proud of — not a rushed version.
Traction — people saying yes, momentum building, proof that it works.
Finally getting it out of my head and into the world, even imperfectly.
Sustainable progress that doesn't cost me my health, relationships, or sense of self.

content:
There is a version of the entrepreneurship story you have heard a hundred times: the founder who burned the boats, bet everything, and built something remarkable from the wreckage of a comfortable life they left behind. It is a compelling story. It is also, for most women carrying a job, a family, and an idea they can't quite silence, a story that does not quite fit.

Nami Prakash's story fits better. And it is far more useful.

The Idea That Wouldn't Wait — But Had To

Nami is the founder of The Mind Quotient, a framework built around developing the human skills that an increasingly automated workplace keeps deprioritizing — and keeps desperately needing. But the business did not begin the day she resigned. It began inside her corporate teams, in the questions she kept asking, in the frameworks she kept reaching for that did not yet have names.

She was building in the margins. Not hiding, not stalling — building. And that distinction matters more than almost anything else in this conversation.

Aimee asks her early on about the pull between the idea and the life surrounding it, and Nami is honest: there was a moment she tried to leave before she was ready. She took a leap that did not land. And rather than frame that as failure, she carries it forward as the most clarifying data point she has. Readiness, she learned, is not a feeling. It is evidence.

What "Moving Deliberately" Actually Looks Like

One of the sharpest distinctions Nami makes — and one that will quietly reorganize the way you think about your own timeline — is the difference between deliberate movement and revision as avoidance. If you are adjusting your messaging for the fifteenth time but have not let a single real person respond to the idea yet, you are not being careful. You are hiding.

She is not saying this to be harsh. She is saying it because she did it too, and she recognized it for what it was: fear wearing the costume of perfectionism.

The answer, she found, was not to quit everything and force momentum. It was to test the idea in the smallest possible way with a real human being — and to let their response, not her own internal revision loop, tell her what to do next. Feedback is not threatening when you have not over-invested in a version that hasn't been tested yet.

Energy Management Is the Actual Work

If you are building something while working full-time, the conversation about time management is almost beside the point. You already know you do not have enough time. What Nami surfaces is a quieter, harder problem: you also do not have unlimited energy, and energy spent in the wrong direction does not come back.

She talks about this practically — how she learned to protect the hours when she was most capable of deep thinking, how she stopped treating all tasks as equal, and how the single-mother context sharpened her relationship with both. When there is genuinely no buffer, you get ruthless about what deserves your best hours. That ruthlessness, she suggests, is not a limitation of her circumstances. It is one of the clearest gifts they gave her.

The Human Skills No One Is Talking About Enough

The Mind Quotient is built on a conviction: that as automation continues to absorb transactional and technical work, the skills that remain irreplaceably human — emotional intelligence, self-awareness, relational depth, adaptive thinking — are not "soft." They are the hardest skills to develop, the last to be automated, and the most urgently undertaught.

Nami talks about what she means by human skills with the kind of precision that makes you realize most conversations on this topic stay comfortably vague. She is not talking about being nice. She is talking about a learnable, measurable, practicable set of capacities that change how you lead, how you parent, and how you show up to every relationship in your life.

MQ Circles are how she is bringing this to scale — not as a course you consume alone, but as a skill, a guided conversation, and a way to embed that learning into daily life. The goal is not information transfer. It is transformation that sticks because it is held in community.

Building Between Cultures, Expectations, and a Memoir

The conversation gets personal in ways that feel earned rather than performed. Nami talks about growing up between cultures, about the inherited definitions of success that shaped her long before she examined them, and about writing a memoir that required her to be vulnerable in public about a private life.

She is clear that writing the memoir and building the business are related acts: both required her to decide whose version of her story she was telling. Both required her to set a boundary — not around ambition, but around other people's relationship to her ambition.

Aimee, who has written about her own life and leads a company while raising six children, meets her there without flinching. This is one of those conversations where both people are actually talking to each other, not performing for the listener — and somehow that makes it more useful to you, not less.

What Do You Believe Enough to Build?

The question Aimee closes with is the one that lingers. Not: do you have the right idea, the right timing, the right market, the right runway. But: what do you believe enough to keep building even when the conditions are imperfect?

Nami's answer is grounded, specific, and unexpectedly freeing. She is not asking you to quit your job. She is not promising that conviction alone is enough. She is pointing at something more nuanced: that the strength of your belief will determine the quality of your patience — and that patience, directed toward the right things, is one of the most underrated forms of ambition there is.

If you are carrying an idea alongside a life that is already full, this conversation will not give you a checklist. It will give you something better — a clearer picture of what you are actually doing, and why it is worth continuing.
